newsitem.title: INDIA: Foreign buyers waver as Indian stocks correct.
newsitem.headline: Foreign buyers waver as Indian stocks correct.

text.p: Foreign portfolio inflows have risen in the past two weeks after India's pro-business budget, but demand is seen wavering as the market undergoes a correction, analysts said on Wednesday.
"FIIs (foreign institutional investors) are waiting for the markets to cool," said Bharat Iyer, market strategist at UBS Securities, the investment arm of Union Bank of Switzerland.
"The (Indian) markets are overbought. So a correction is under way," he said.

The FIIs made net purchases of $101.1 million during March 1-12 after the February 28 budget for 1997/98 (April-March) cut corporate and personal taxes and raised foreign portfolio limits in firms to 30 percent from 24 percent.
The inflows in February totalled $88.8 million and in January they were $89.3 million, figures with the Securities and Exchange Board of India show.
"They (the FIIs) are not able to enter because the index ran away," said Vimesh Zaveri, vice president (operations) at KBS Capital Management Ltd, a brokerage that caters to FIIs.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's top-30 index leapt nearly 16 percent to a 4,029.56 high from the pre-budget close of 3,474.79 before the rally ran out of steam.
The index was trading 91.71 points, or 2.42 percent, lower at 3,703.46 on Wednesday afternoon.
"FIIs are selective buyers," said Zaveri. "I expect them to become very aggressive buyers at 3,650 (index level)."
Analysts expect the FIIs to pump in about $4.5-$5.0 billion in calendar 1997 against $4.5 billion in 1996.
UBS's Iyer said attractive valuations would be the key factor luring foreign money into Indian stocks over the next few months.
"The budget has provided a strong impetus to kick start earnings," he said.
The budget cut corporate taxes to 35 percent from 40 percent and removed a 7.5 percent surcharge on the tax.
Net profits of Indian firms are forecast to rise 24 percent on average in fiscal 1997/98 against a mixed bag of negative growth to earnings increase of 5-10 percent for 1996/97, he said.

Fresh FII inflows would be influenced by how primary issues pick up. The government-run overseas telecommunications monopoly Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd is holding roadshows for a $570 million global depositary receipts issue.
Iyer expects more such offerings mopping up FII allocations.
